theory.title: CDN & Caching: Content Closer to You
theory.recap: DNS translates a domain name into an IP address. Load balancers distribute traffic across servers. A CDN combines both ideas: DNS resolves your domain to the nearest CDN edge, and the edge serves cached content instead of forwarding to the origin.
theory.plainObjective: DNS resolves the domain to the CDN's IP. At the CDN router, read the routing table: the most-specific prefix leads to the cached edge copy. Route there.
theory.summary: CDNs work because cached content is served from a node geographically close to you, reducing latency from hundreds of milliseconds to single digits. The Cache-Control header on the response tells caches how long to store content before fetching a fresh copy from origin.

bodyParagraphs.heading: What a CDN does
bodyParagraphs.text: A Content Delivery Network stores copies of content on servers (edge nodes) close to end users. When you load an image, the nearest CDN edge serves it - not a server across the world.

bodyParagraphs.heading: Cache-Control
bodyParagraphs.text:
The origin server sets Cache-Control headers to tell caches how long to keep content:
  • max-age=3600 - fresh for one hour, serve from cache
  • no-cache - always revalidate with origin before serving
  • no-store - never cache this response

bodyParagraphs.heading: Cache HIT vs MISS
bodyParagraphs.text: A cache HIT means the edge has a fresh copy - response is instant. A cache MISS means the edge must fetch from origin. The first user always triggers a MISS; everyone after gets a HIT until the content expires.

bodyParagraphs.heading: Routing: most-specific prefix wins
bodyParagraphs.text: The CDN router uses longest-prefix matching. The edge cache has a more specific route (/24) than the origin fallback (/16). Your destination falls in the /24 range, so the CDN routes you to the edge.

theory.mission:
Your packet requests api.example.com (port 80). DNS resolves it to 10.60.1.5 - a CDN edge address.

At the CDN router, the routing table has two entries. Read them carefully. The longer prefix leads to the edge cache (cache HIT). The shorter prefix is the origin fallback. Route to the edge.

termIntroductions.headline: CDN
termIntroductions.body: A Content Delivery Network is a global system of edge servers that cache copies of content near end users. Instead of every request traveling to one central origin server, the CDN serves from the nearest edge. DNS routes you to the nearest CDN node automatically.

termIntroductions.headline: DNS resolves to CDN
termIntroductions.body: api.example.com resolved to 10.60.1.5 - a CDN edge IP. The CDN operator configured DNS to return edge IPs instead of the origin. Often different users in different regions get different IPs from the same domain - the nearest edge node.

termIntroductions.headline: Cache HIT
termIntroductions.body: The edge node had a fresh cached copy (max-age=3600 was still valid). Response served in <5ms instead of the 120ms round trip to origin. This is why CDNs matter: static assets like images, JS, and CSS can be cached for hours or days.

termIntroductions.headline: Cache MISS
termIntroductions.body: The CDN had to fetch from origin - either the content expired or was never cached here. The /16 route is less specific than /24, so this is the fallback path. Your destIP (10.60.1.5) actually fits the /24 prefix - go back and take the more-specific route.
